description: We’re a team from AUBH. We’re taking on the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge: an interactive game where students run a lunar or Martian outpost and balance life support, power, radiation shielding, and food to keep their crew alive, all based on real NASA data.
summary: exolife is a 3D mission trainer game for kids, built for the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge. Players run the South Pole Outpost on the Moon and keep their crew alive by balancing four systems: air, water, food and power. When something goes wrong, such as a clogged air filter, they find the cause, fix it and learn the real science behind the fix. Nova, an in-game mission manager, guides each step with three levels of hints, so no child is left stuck. Every fact card in the game is labelled and cites its NASA or Canadian Space Agency source, so kids learn things they can trust. Each mission ends with a debrief that scores time, mistakes and hints, and states in one sentence what the child learned. This matters because kids usually learn about space by reading, while astronauts learn by training. exolife lets the next generation practise living off Earth before they ever leave it.
details:
What it does and how it works
Exolife is a desktop game for Windows and macOS. Players start on a 3D solar-system map, select the Moon, and enter a cutaway habitat with three rooms: Living Quarters, Equipment Bay, and Storage. Four gauges (air, water, food, power) drain over time and are linked to each other. For example, low power slows the air machine. Players use tools and stored supplies to fix problems, and the crew reacts with thought bubbles and changing needs (energy, hunger, fitness).

Two missions are fully playable:

  • Mission 1, “First Morning on the Moon”: a tutorial covering the gauges, food, exercise, and the daily plan.
  • Mission 2, “The Stuffy Cabin”: the player diagnoses falling air quality and replaces a dirty air filter.

Sixteen more missions, Mars and Proxima Centauri, are designed and appear in the game as “Coming Soon.”

Benefits and intended impact

  • Kids learn by doing instead of memorising, which makes the science stick.
  • Every fact is sourced and labelled, so the game never presents an invented game number as a NASA fact.
  • The debrief gives teachers and parents a measurable view of progress.
  • Our goal is to spark interest in space careers and STEM by making life support, power, and resource management feel personal, ahead of Artemis-era lunar living.

Tools and technologies

  • Game: Godot 4 engine, written in GDScript, exported for macOS and Windows. It runs offline with local autosave.
  • AI assistance: Claude by Anthropic (Claude Code), used to help write and debug game code and to draft design documents. The team set the scope, design, content, and testing.
  • Website: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages, with downloads via GitHub Releases.
  • Design: custom logos and brand; Hanken Grotesk and JetBrains Mono fonts (open source).

Creativity

  • A child-friendly interface inspired by real mission control, where each gauge shows a face so the youngest players can read the crew’s status at a glance.
  • Nova’s three-step hint system (Nudge, Clue, Show me) builds independence instead of giving answers away.
  • Cause-and-effect systems mean one problem can lead to another, just like on a real base.
  • Fact cards appear on loading screens and on objects, so learning is built into play.

Factors we considered
Age-appropriate language and difficulty, scientific accuracy with clear labels for what is real and what is simplified, accessibility through Nova modes (full guide, hints only, off), short missions that fit a classroom period, a scope that is small but fully working, and ethical design that motivates through learning rather than pressure.
